utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Cepic will now continue. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] Mr. Drewienkiewicz, in your statement in paragraph 111 you stated that on the 31st of December, 1988 -- 1998, you learned that the KLA had declared the year 1999 the year of independence of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When you heard such an announcement, I suppose that you took some steps in order to defuse the tensions and the threats which such an announcement on the part of the KLA actually entailed, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did was treat it with extreme skepticism because I've heard of these years of liberation before and it didn't work either this time, did it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to explain this to me. You were unable to take any measures vis-a-vis the KLA, even by -- in the sense of just warning them in relation to announcements of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, it appeared in the media. As such, I noted it and that was really it. I certainly didn't run out on my own account to issue press statements. I treated it with the skepticism that it deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand your answer, but my question was: Did you try at all to get in touch, to establish any contact with KLA representatives in relation to that particular matter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in charge of the media policy for the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission. It was one of the few things I wasn't in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, for your answer. When you were giving testimony, the Prosecutor exhibited Exhibit P634 -- actually, asked for it to be admitted and that is a chronology of the most important developments in the period in which your mission was active in Kosovo and Metohija and under serial number 116 in that document it is noted that 15 companies of the Army of Yugoslavia were observed in the barracks. Do you know perhaps where these 15 companies were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word is they were noted as being out of barracks, which was the significance of the entry because under the Clark agreement there were only three positions out of barracks where companies were allowed to be, and three companies would broadly be about 400 soldiers. And that shorthand of 15 VJ companies out of barracks was shorthand for us -- my people having observed something between 1500 and 2.000 VJ soldiers out of barracks in positions in the countryside, which equated to about 15 companies' worth. And so about 12 companies' worth more than were allowed for under the Clark agreement. That's the point of -- that's the meaning behind that shorthand statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But do you know perhaps where these 12 companies were located?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, it was about 12 companies' worth of people, so it wasn't necessarily 12 locations, I think it was more like 20. But now, eight years later, certainly not. I do know that my verifiers, of whom by this stage there were 1200 scattered all over Kosovo, had brought in -- had reported what they had seen; and when that was all added up, it came to that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. Would you please be so kind as to give me briefer answers, and I shall try to be more to the point and more specific when I put my questions to you. What would you say if I told you that nine companies in this period, which is the end of February/the beginning of March 1999, they were performing depth security of the border, of the state border, because of the frequent incidents which occurred. That was not a breach of the agreement because this was the border belt.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the border belt wasn't defined, but it was generally accepted by then as being 5 kilometres, and around about that time there was a decision taken in Belgrade to widen the border to 10 kilometres without any consultation with us. If you're telling me that you're now, on behalf of the people at the time, making a report that because of the situation on the border you are contemplating increasing the security up there, that's precisely the sort of report I'd have quite liked to have got at the time. It's a bit late, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do agree, General, sir, that it is a bit too late now. It is way too late for many things now. So these nine companies that are performing depth security of the border and three companies which were in regular training, Batlava the position near Prizren which you toured with Colonel Delic and another location, another position, near Prizren actually amount to this number of 15 -- 15 companies out of barracks, which is according to the spirit of the agreement. Do you perhaps now -- can you perhaps now recall these locations when I tell them where they were actually?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would want to go to a map and I would want to go through all my reports. But it doesn't matter whether now -- or to me it doesn't matter because at the time this was not made clear. If there had been a properly argued case made that because of the situation on the border it was necessary to move units out of barracks, that would have been a perfectly reasonable discussion to have had, and we would have reported it back to the OSCE, who would probably have discussed it with NATO and the decision would have been made one way or the other. That's precisely the thing that could have happened in an ideal situation, but unfortunately it didn't. It was all unilateral action that we only found out about by chance after the event which was not in the spirit of the agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the registrar please show us Prosecutor's Exhibit P2536. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, we can see your notes and annotations, talking points for Belgrade meeting on the 27th of November, 1998. And the third paragraph you know that the FRY, especially VJ units, have established a record of good implementation of Article 4 of the arms control agreement. We know that for this to be the case steps had to be taken to ensure that units throughout the VJ were informed of the obligations of Article 4 of the agreement. And this actually refers to the Naumann-Clark agreement of the 25th of October, 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Article 4 arms control agreement is a reference to an OSCE arms control agreement, which is a subregional agreement. My point in making this was to attempt to make the meeting as positive as possible by indicating areas where it was possible for -- for FRY to meet obligations and to try to build on that common ground to move -- to move the situation forward. But it was nothing -- that third bullet was nothing to do with the Naumann-Clark agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You added here by hand "use Naumann-Clark," so a paragraph above, above the text which I read out.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And if -- my note to myself is to the effect that I propose that we use the Naumann-Clark agreement as the basis, although if you, General, feel there's a better way than I'm very interested to hear of it. In other words, let's talk about this, let's have a discussion, and let's agree a way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This article which I quoted, the tense which is used is the past tense, namely that the Army of Yugoslavia, the FRY, had already established a record of good implementation of Article 4. So it is not something which was to be, but something that had already been done.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a group of officers in Vienna whose only job it was to run the Article 4 arms control agreement. And I was simply making the point that it's perfectly possible to -- to carry out a series of inspections. I was drawing his attention to the -- a protocol that existed that everyone was familiar with that we could take as a start point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the KDOM mission had previously performed over 30 armament verifications in Kosovo, which all went smoothly without a single objection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. And again, I draw your attention to the fact that the KDOM mission wasn't one KDOM mission. It was a number of missions reporting independently to their embassies in Belgrade, which very loosely coordinated with one another and certainly didn't share reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about their official report, and Mr. Ciaglinski also confirmed that he had partly examined the file where it is -- where the confirmation of these verifications, of these inspections, is actually noted. Do you have knowledge of that, Mr. Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. I'm at a loss to know which file that was because Mr. Ciaglinski only arrived in early December. I mean, if he told you, I don't dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. You also said that in December you were unable to inspect, to tour, the barracks in Pristina. That is in paragraph 80 of your statement. Later you did visit a number of installations, a number of facilities, did you not, Mr. Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I visited or my people visited the deployed locations. We were not ever allowed into the Pristina barracks until, I think, about mid-March for a meeting and we went into the Prizren barracks for a meeting which should have been an inspection of the barracks but which wasn't allowed by the commander on the ground. So I went into two barracks, but not to perform the inspections that I had wished to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your verifiers had a large number of verifications of facilities, barracks, and positions of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were ever allowed into barracks in order to carry out proper inspections, no. It would have been reported to me very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a large number of meetings were held between representatives of the Pristina Corps and your mission's verifiers, whereby cooperation between the two parties was significantly promoted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean, that was our intention at every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you said a moment ago that you got access to the Pristina barracks in mid-March, was that for a proper inspection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. We were summoned into the barracks and were introduced to another -- another group of liaison -- liaison officers from the Yugoslav army, who were to replace the ones that we had spent a considerable amount of time building up a relationship with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, did you ever submit a written request to the effect that you wanted to inspect, to visit, the barracks in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either written or it was delivered verbally to General Loncar. It was certainly the meeting -- the specific purpose of a meeting with General Loncar, and I do actually now recall that it was -- it was mentioned in a letter as well. So the answer is yes to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your verifiers and representatives of the army worked together on a procedure for the touring of units, so they worked together to establish a procedure for the inspection of units and that they did together?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, that was to go around the deployed locations, the locations out of barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you are aware of the fact that not a single of those positions that were barracks could not be seen without liaison officer, an army liaison officer, as well as a liaison officer of the KVM. Was that not so, Mr. Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think this is -- maybe it's the translation but the question is unclear. I mean, the witness has said that what could be visited were deployments outside the barracks. And then there's a-- yeah, the question reads strangely, I think. We need to clarify whether we're talking about access to barracks or units outside the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the English translation is unclear, so could you ask that again, please, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, do you know that access to any unit of the Army of Yugoslavia was possible only if there was a liaison officer there, both liaison officer of the Yugoslav army as well as a liaison officer representing the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was -- that was what we wanted, yes, that each liaison officer from the Yugoslav side would have an -- a counterpart on the KVM side. And we had no difficulty meeting that person and saying, Okay, let's go and look at a unit. We didn't have any problem with that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. That was one of the reasons why new officers had been brought to Pristina, those who could speak English and to whom you delivered a lecture, if I'm not wrong, on the 16th of March, 1999, in order to establish easier communication between the units of the army on the one hand and representatives of the Kosovo Verification Mission on the other.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time that I've ever been told that the reason these officers were given to us was -- was because they could speak English, and I certainly don't recall them making that clear at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was a very short time for that to become clear, because four days later, on the 20th, you actually left Kosovo, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would say it takes about eight seconds to say, Hello, I speak English, how nice to see you, and I don't recall that happening. I recall interpreters being used for translation throughout, as it always had been. The reason we were given -- the reason we were given for these new officers was because the previous liaison officers had become too cooperative with us. Let's be quite clear on this. This was not a huggy-feely sort of relationship. By this stage, an extremely -- a relationship that was full of tension, this was mid-March. We were about to be ordered out because of the safety to our people. So I would not want this meeting to be misrepresented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How did you know on the 16th of March that you were to leave Kosovo soon, shortly, Mr. Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was a topic of almost minute-by-minute discussion with -- with the people in Vienna and with our NATO counterparts. And if it had been left to them, they would have ordered us out about two weeks earlier, and we were hanging on by -- at our request because we felt we could still be of use. But if it had been left to Vienna, they would have certainly have ordered us out on about the 5th of March, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Whose decision was it for you to leave Kosovo? Was it a decision from Vienna or from your headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an order from the chairman in office in Vienna, who was the foreign minister of Norway, Knut Vollebaek.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Drewienkiewicz, is your assertion that there was an occasional excessive use of force, was it based on the number of soldiers on one side and on the other side? Was that the basis for such an assertion on your part? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The excessive use of force was -- the words I used were disproportionate, and what I meant was using heavy weapons to deal with snipers and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But actually you did not know what the real number of soldiers on the other side was in these operations, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General Loncar also testified before this Tribunal, and he actually refuted the allegations that there had been excessive use of force. He stressed that you had raised such an objection -- that you would raise such an objection, even when one or two policemen were used in actions on the part of the police forces of Serbia, and that you never clearly specified in what instances and on what locations and why such an excessive use of force was resorted to, and that was Mr. Loncar's testimony before this Court, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. Mr. Ciaglinski also testified before this Court, and the few operations that the army undertook in Kosovo were, in his view, in accordance with all standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't think a question has been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Probably -- possibly because you interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Cepic, and we're waiting in excitement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, colleague Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, in view of the fact that I was interrupted as I was about to ask my question, you heard me what I said. Could you give me please your comment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now a question has not been asked. There has been a long monologue of a lot of propositions stated by my colleague and no question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree. A question is clear to Mr. Drewienkiewicz. If he cannot answer because he's unclear about what's being asked, he'll tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm happy to comment. The discussion about disproportionate use of force was a perpetual topic of conversation between General Loncar and myself, and I think at almost every meeting I would deliver a short statement or tirade or lecture about it. The sort of thing I drew attention to at the time was the use of tank main armament being fired into villages when there had been one or two rifle shots fired out of it. And my point time and time again was that it's not a very good way -- it's not a very efficient way of dealing with the problem because you're going to create more problems than you solve, because these heavy weapons don't just kill the person they're aimed at even if they hit them at the time; they kill a lot of other bystanders and it gets you in trouble. This is why a disproportionate use of force is such a bad idea. I can assure you -- and if we go to my various notebooks and the records that were made of the various conversations with General Loncar by his people and by my people, we will find it was a persistent area of discussion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I invested a great deal of effort to try and locate a single report on the part of the mission which would mention excessive use of force, and I wasn't successful. Can you assist me in telling me whether there is a report in existence of excessive use of force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Cepic has been using "excessive" throughout rather than "disproportionate."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can -- I am sure if we go back through the reports we will find statements made at the time making the point about excessive or disproportionate use of force against particularly villages, built-up areas where there were civilians who were not identified as being members of the KLA. I can personally recall moments when I was present when tank main armament was fired into villages, and I was rather closer to it than I meant to be at the time, to be honest. But yes, I can recall those -- such moments. So I do not believe that this is an issue. I think if we take the trouble to go back, then we'll find plenty of examples of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps one of such examples could be cited now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the registrar to put P621 up on e-court, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, we have a letter sent by you to the Federal Commission to General Loncar on February 3rd, 1999. Inter alia you mentioned on page 1, paragraph 1, that on the 21st of January, 1999, the village of Planeja was shelled and subsequently looted. I believe you gained this information from your associates. I presume you did not attend the scene yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In assessment by the regional centres of the KVM, or rather, concerning their assessments, you stated that the regional centre in Prizren was the best of all the regional centres. Do you still stand by your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it produced the best reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to get to the question, Mr. Cepic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the registrar to show us P673, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that's it on the screen. Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 starting with Planeja. This is the report of the Prizren regional centre we've just mentioned. In that paragraph we see the following: "A report received by CC2," CC being control centre, "on 27 January, 1999, that the villagers of Planeja had informed the VJ that they would have to vacate their homes," as read out by Mr. Cepic, "was to be investigated by a CC2 patrol today. CS21," I believe it stands for call signal, "dispatched to Planeja. They report that the village was quiet and there was no VJ check-point or presence outside or inside the village. The only shooting that the villagers reported was a shooting incident between 1800 and 1830 hours on 24 January 1999 with no casualties reported. The villagers did not hear any shooting during the night of the 27th January 1999. "On the way out of the village, CS21 met a bus full of people heading into Planeja" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the question? We can read this if necessary. What is the question you want the witness to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This will also be my last question with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, doesn't this differ quite significantly, I mean the difference between the report you received and the report drafted by the regional centre of the verification mission, that actually there were no incidents in the village of Planeja as a matter of fact. Isn't that so, Mr. Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree. You've shown me two reports. It would not just have been that report. I'm not sure the dates tally, but even if they do there would have been a number of reports. I would not have put an allegation into a letter to General Loncar that was not supported by fact or by report. And so there would have been reports, and you can -- you could see from the -- from my original letter to General Loncar that if it was unconfirmed, I said it was unconfirmed. The point at that stage was actually producing chapter and verse about the allegations of looting, which was a moment when General Loncar expressed complete incredulity and said that he couldn't believe such a thing and would I please produce chapter and verse, and so off we went and we produced chapter and verse. So each of these statements would have been supported at the time by -- by reports. I had -- you know, I had quite a lot of people working for me to do precisely this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, what's the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken I think that the first document that was shown concerned looting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was just about to ask to see the other document again because I hadn't followed the point, it was so convoluted. And I just wanted to see what the first document actually said. Can we see it again, please, so that we can compare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P621, 621. [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is the comparable statement in this document that you say is inconsistent with the statement in P673?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave in the first report it is stated that the village had been shelled and looted. In the second report a few days later, a patrol of the KVM established all that and they inquired of the villagers whether there was any shooting, and they only said that the -- on the 27th there was some shooting between 6.00 and 6.30 p.m. without casualties and that the villagers did not hear any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I remember what was said in it, but you'll see that this one is dealing with the 21st and the 24th. And the 24th is the one day to which -- on which it said in the later report that -- or at least in P673 that shooting took place. Now, what's the inconsistency you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, in my humble opinion, I believe the villagers would have reported any damage following shelling or looting. Instead, they only reported a far more significant incident with a shooting. On the 24th, the only incident was the shooting where there were no casualties. If that seems more important than looting and shelling, well, it seems illogical. The only thing -- the only incident reported was this, otherwise the villagers must have -- or would have reported any looting or shooting. They were actually able to specify the exact time of this incident. This is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic, for that explanation. Thank you very much. That completes your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] This is the last question. I haven't gotten any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. Just to reply in English because you said "Dobar dan" in Serbian language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, I saw for the first time, I think after your evidence began, a reference to tanks using blank ammunition, something hadn't particularly crossed my mind. It may not be in your evidence, but there is a reference certainly somewhere in the evidence we have in this case. Did that actually happen that tanks would use blanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, certainly, sir. The ones I saw weren't blanks, and the ones that were -- I can't ever remember someone saying that tanks used blanks. They were jolly good blanks if they were because they were synchronised with explosions at the other end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had a number of witnesses make allegations of apparently endless shelling of their village by heavy weaponry, but then be unable to specify what damage was done and it's something that we're -- at least I, speaking for myself, have been having some difficulty with. Could you help me to understand that concept that a village can be shelled all day and no damage done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it takes a lot of shells to knock down a house because that's not the purpose of the weapons is. The purpose of the weapons is to go through the armour of another tank, obviously. And the tank rounds aren't necessarily best designed for use on buildings, which are obviously more soft-skinned. So it's quite possible in some cases that the tank round goes through and out the other side and all you've got is a hole the one side and a hole the other side and if we're lucky nobody's standing in the middle. So we did go to villages, we did see the results. Artillery was more effective than tank fire in terms of producing noticeable damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may also be a problem created by translation, of course. The commonplace use of the expression "shelling" may not be an accurate description of what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was certainly moments when, you know, groups of artillery -- artillery guns of six at a time, which would be their normal -- four or six would be their normal tactical grouping were seen lined up alongside the road firing. Now, the range of those guns is often several kilometres, so it's quite difficult to see them firing and be at the other end on the impact at the same time. And I wasn't very keen for my people to be where they impacted either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But these are weapons you define different from tanks. These are smaller artillery --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These would be towed artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would they damage a house in a different way from a shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What damage would they do to a house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are high trajectory so they would come in from above and typically would come in through the roof, whereas a tank fires -- it fires its shell much faster and so it goes in a straight line. So tank -- tank fire tends to be line of sight, whereas artillery is an area weapon directed several kilometres away not necessarily at something you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting us with that diversion. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Drewienkiewicz, I am Dan Ivetic and I am representing Mr. Sreten Lukic and I have some questions for you. I would like you to clear up an area that caused us confusion and consternation yesterday concerning the KDOMs and the establishment of a base-line number for the forces in Kosovo-Metohija. First of all, sir, am I correct that prior to the Kosovo Verifiers Mission being up and running in Kosovo, the various KDOMs under the unofficial leadership of the US-KDOM initially handled the verification tasks required under the agreements, and in fact negotiated the -- what has been called the Burns-Djordjevic agreement which is an annex to the KVM agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They operated in a pretty loose coordination. They did do whatever verification they did because they were the people that had been asked to do it and they did produce the Burns-Djordjevic agreement which was about MUP check-points, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that you had contact with Mr. Sean Burns, who was the head of the US-KDOM. And in the course of your -- I'd like to ask you, in the course of your contact and communications with Mr. Sean Burns, did you ever hear or become aware of the fact that the Serbian MUP provided detailed tables and documents to KDOM, identifying all force levels needed to establish a base-line already in October, specifically 29 October 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it then that you would be surprised, that is to say that during the several months you were in Kosovo you never heard of the fact that the US-KDOM issued a written report in Pristina on the 27th of December [Realtime transcript read in error "September"], 1998, establishing the base-line of permitted MUP personnel in Kosovo at 10.021 persons. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never ever saw or heard of that document, and I can categorically state that I don't think I ever received one piece of paper from the US-KDOM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, did you say 27th September?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I thought you did. It's September in the transcript. It should be December. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear this number, 10.021 personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's such a specific number that I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness are kindly reminded to pause between question and answer for the sake of interpreters and the court reporter, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I presume you got the same message I did so we should both try and be a little bit more appreciative of the interpreters in this case. Did you know from your presence in Kosovo of KDOM personnel physically counting Serbian forces and Yugoslav forces that were withdrawing from Kosovo in the last few months of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- you're talking I think, so we don't get confusing each other, you're talking about the end of October 1998 when some MUP and quite a lot of FRY military, FRY army, withdrew from Kosovo. I don't think you're talking about the situation after the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I know that they were there on the ground to do it, and I know that there were then reports that were then taken as adequate. I didn't ever see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At that time was the KVM up and running as an operational organ in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was brought into being at the -- in the middle of October, and it was simply a gleam in somebody's eye. There were no people for it, nobody had been asked to provide people. There was no equipment, no vehicles. God Almighty himself could not have produced 12 apostles in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I would like to move back briefly to some questions relating to your background. I think we'll be going through these rather quickly. I've seen from your various information provided with your statement that you have a military career. Am I correct that your professional career does not include any experience working as a civilian police officer in any capacity, or a policeman I should say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a policeman but in my time in Bosnia, I worked closely with the people that were dealing with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I correct that you did not have any specific or formal police training with respect to your appointment to the OSCE-KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when it comes to technical details about the operation structure and functioning of the Serbian MUP police, in all fairness you would not consider yourself an expert and would have to defer to someone with more knowledge. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say that as a result of my time in Bosnia which was 20 months very recently before this, I was fairly familiar with the way police operated in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the MUP in the Republic of Bosnia, that is to say at both the Federation level and the Republika Srpska, are structured differently than the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there are differences in structure. I'm talking about the way they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, within the OS-KVM mission there were dedicated police observers and verifiers. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who had initially been put forth as deputy head of the KVM specifically for police and judicial matters, whose appointment Mr. Walker rejected?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that a name was put forward and that there was some concern in the OSCE in Vienna, which was more than just Walker. It was general concern, and as a result of that the country concerned withdrew his name and provided a more suitable candidate, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the more suitable candidate, I presume, is Judge Kessler from Italy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to Judge Kessler who was appointed to the KVM as the deputy head for police and judicial matters, do you know what his duties and activities were relative to the police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean prior to his arriving?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I mean during the course of the KVM mission. We have not heard anything about him in your testimony so I would like to find out how much, if anything, you know about his activities in relation to the police in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he arrived in, I think, very late January and at that point I gave everything I -- everything I could to him on policing matters because clearly it was his portfolio, not mine. We were very short of ex-policemen or seconded policemen. We had hardly any at the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- I apologise, sir. I'm slowing down for purposes of the translators, who I hear are still speaking with respect to our previous discussion. Am I correct, sir, that indeed you had asked for additional police verifiers to be assigned, but in fact that you were unsuccessful in that endeavour?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of my constant refrains that we needed police as many as we could, as quickly as we could, and we were not very successful in getting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, flowing from that am I correct that there was an issue within the KVM because some of the verifiers that were on the ground were not properly trained and inexperienced, particularly on the police side, because they had not had the requisite training that would be required for that field?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. What they were supposed to do is sort of sit in Vienna for about six months until they were ready. We were doing the best we could with the people we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As a result of the foregoing, did you become aware of situations where events were misreported because certain verifiers did not go to verify things first-hand but relied upon second-hand information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. I was always concerned that people should go as far forward as possible, and they sometimes had to be nudged gently to go further forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've testified about the confusion and problem caused by the continued existence of a separate US-KDOM operation. I'd like to ask you now about the components of the US-KDOM that were absorbed into the KVM. Did there at any point in time appear to be US-KDOM personnel operating at odds with the rest of the KVM mission, as if working on a separate agenda?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the -- first of all, there was a very high turnover of the US-KDOM in -- between mid-November and the end of December. And so they had almost nobody left who had been there in the summer. At that stage, we were given about two-thirds of the US-KDOM people, and the remainder remained as a separate entity, as I understand it providing support to Ambassador Chris Hill, who of course continued to come into the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as a result of having a -- of not having enough verifiers, having some verifiers that were lacking experience or training, and having this huge turnover of US-KDOM personnel, am I correct that at some point in time during the mission you concluded that you were receiving incorrect and biased field reports in favour of the Albanian or KLA side, and thereafter assigned specific trusted personnel to go into the field to verify certain of the reports you had received. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it as specifically as that. I would say that there were moments when I was concerned about the accuracy, and I had always kept a couple of patrols that I used as my reserve to go out to -- to areas that seemed particularly difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a slightly different point, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's being asked is whether you were conscious of bias.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was bias in -- yes, I mean, there was bias throughout the report because everybody comes from somewhere. And so some of the people that came from -- from some countries thought that the KLA had more right on their side, and some thought that the Serb authorities had more right on their side. That was a fact. And it was our job to try to steer a course between them. This was not an entirely one-way street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall at some point in time during the existence of your mission on -- in Kosovo-Metohija that you asked or assigned Christopher John Clark, a warrant officer in the British Army seconded to the KVM to go out in the field and to double-check or verify certain of the reports that you had received that you felt may be biased?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him and I certainly used him. He was an explosive ordnance disposal expert and where there were reports of particular devices, he had the technical expertise to know the difference between a hand-grenade and a satchel bomb. That was the sort of thing I used him for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's try to be clear. So the answer to the question is no, really, is it? That he wasn't somebody you used to investigate cases where you suspected bias?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move on. I've got approximately six or so questions relating to Racak that I'd like to just touch on a few points about. First of all, am I correct that based upon the information available to the OSCE-KVM, there was in fact a KLA presence in Racak itself and a KLA base a mere 1.5 kilometres from Racak in the village of Topola?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came -- when I went into Racak for the first time on the Saturday, there were no KLA present. In the course of my time in that village that afternoon, KLA appeared in uniform. So they were present. I personally noted a trenchline dug within 500 metres of the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, prior to undertaking their operation in Racak to arrest elements of the KLA, the local police officials in Stimlje and Urosevac not only gave notice of their operation to the KVM but engaged in lengthy discussions with the local KVM personnel regarding the same. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that may be correct, but I was not aware of that at the time and it was certainly not reported to us. The -- I think the individual had just arrived and was not acting as he should have done. And I don't think he spoke English very well and I don't think he understood what he was being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you recall whether Warrant Officer Clark and David Meyer of the KVM may have had any discussions with personnel regarding the upcoming Racak investigation with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would -- you -- would you be surprised to find that Warrant Officer Clark gave a statement, a sworn statement, to the Office of the Prosecutor, it's Exhibit 6D106 that we've utilised previously in this case, in which he specifically said that the commander of the Stimlje police station had lengthy discussions with David Meyer regarding the situation, that it was a known planned event that the MUP were going to Racak, and notice was given to KVM officially and indeed that notice was given the day before the Racak operation actually took place, and that the KVM personnel had instructed two KVM vehicles to accompany the police patrol, but that those KVM vehicles disobeyed their instructions and stayed at the Stimlje police station. Do you recall any of those events, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, you just answered my question, whether you recall any of those events.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me, please, what the MUP said they were going to do in Racak? Presumably they were going to do a bit of community policing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, they were going to go in and arrest the KLA, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if only they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the KLA attacked and prevented the investigating judge from reaching the scene to perform an on-site investigation. Isn't it correct that the KVM was in the area and indeed, Ambassador Walker was still present?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now on to Saturday, you're on to Saturday afternoon. Walker and myself are in the village. Walker is in the mosque discussing what to do next with the elders, and while that is going on the judge apparently attempts to come into the village. I was not aware that that was going on until gun-fire erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After that, though, you did not try to convince the KLA to permit the investigation to take place, is that correct, so that no investigation by the investigating judge was able to proceed at the site in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I have known that it was the investigating judge or anybody else who was coming in? I'm sitting in a village with high walls and I hear gun-fire, and I'm supposed to work out that that is heralding the arrival of a judge whom I should now run out into the middle of a fire-fight to welcome. No, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I said thereafter, sir, wasn't it the job of the KVM to liaise with the Serb authorities and to liaise with the KLA. Are you telling us that even with the deputy head of mission and the head of mission in a location, that you were unable to control or have any impact upon the KLA, so as to permit a lawful investigation of the scene?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that I was aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please. Hold on, please. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think the witness just said that he did not know that there was an investigation being carried out and therefore putting to him that he should have somehow -- repeating essentially that he should have done something to allow the inspection to go on, I don't think will take us anywhere and I think the witness has explained why he couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think this is a different approach that the witness can perfectly, competently deal with, and therefore I will repel that objection. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I became aware that the judge wanted to go into Racak, it was the next morning. And I then spent two and a half hours with the judge discussing how we could help her to get into the village without re-igniting the fighting. And I made offers to facilitate her going in so that she could do her job, which I fully acknowledged she needed to be able to do, in a way that was safe for everybody and it was going to be done with my verifiers who were a neutral force in this area. She completely refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your verifiers were unarmed, weren't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be at all surprised that a civilian judge who had just been shot at would be hesitant to go back to the location with unarmed OSCE verifiers who themselves, I believe, a couple days thereafter had been -- were shot at but had been shot at previously by the KLA as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the way the conversation went. The way the conversation went was that she absolutely refused to go anywhere without a MUP escort; and if she was shot at, then the MUP would shoot back. And if that started World War III I could have a nice day. That was more or less the upshot of it. We have a transcript of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to also clear up a couple of points relating to the incident at Rogovo in the Djakovica municipality. Now, first of all, sir, you -- although you did not mention it in your direct testimony I don't believe, am I correct that the information available to the KVM, indeed it's something that you have referenced in your annexure DZ1 to your statement, that in fact the Rogovo site was believed to be a KLA safe house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we found that out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified in your statement that you arrived at the Rogovo scene at approximately 1320 hours on the day of the incident. Isn't it a fact that the incident itself occurred at around 6.30 in the morning, almost seven hours before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And isn't it also true that prior to your arrival there were other KVM staff present who followed the events that were unfolding and would -- who would thus be better able to describe and ascertain the investigative efforts that were underway?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they made written statements to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm told we again have to slow down for the interpreters, so I apologise for my pause. Now, you described -- sorry, we're still waiting for the translation to catch up. Sir, you described -- okay. You describe what you termed as "special police in grey boiler suits or overalls." Isn't it a fact that these persons in these grey boiler suits were collecting the bodies after the conclusion of the scene investigation and were wearing plastic gloves along with their grey overalls?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the paragraph number, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph number for the grey suits, one moment, Your Honour. I know that's something that had come up in questions Your Honour had asked as to what was a overall. I believe it's 165, Your Honour, I'm going to turn to there right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know it's part of the qualifications for this job to be out of touch, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I do know what an overall is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 166. You had asked for him to describe them. That's how he described them. It's paragraph 166 of the marked Drewienkiewicz statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- now, sir, do you recall, in fact, that these individuals in these overalls, coveralls, or boiler suits, whatever we call them, were, in fact, wearing these over regular clothing or uniforms so as not to allow them to become soiled while performing the arduous task of clearing the terrain of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And one of the reasons -- A, they looked very like special forces to me; but B, the -- one of them who had been killed in the fire-fight was also wearing his grey boiler suit when I viewed his body, when I was shown his body. So you're not suggesting they arrived in their cleaning-up gear before they went over the wall, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a videotape that we'll be going through with another witness, so we'll see where that ends up at that point in time. Now, with respect to Rogovo, am I correct that the KVM received a detailed briefing from both the MUP liaison and from General Loncar regarding the incident, as per the compliance with the KVM agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received a briefing. I was briefed by General Loncar. We had a discussion about it, yes. I wouldn't say it was a particularly detailed briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be safe to say that since you were not dealing with the police verifier aspect of the mission, that the -- you are not aware of what briefings were given to the actual MUP liaison officers within the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that -- they in turn reported, and we -- I saw all the reports, and I wouldn't say that they were full briefings. They were briefings. They were -- I can recall them in some detail, but they weren't particularly informative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to just ask a couple of questions to clarify the issue relating to some of your testimony relating to the use of ambulances, in particular I think we're talking about the incident -- well, let me ask you this way. You described that as a result of the Serbs not permitting you the use of a medevac helicopter you had to utilise ground ambulances and when your KVM personnel were wounded on duty they would be driven, wounded, to the border and the Serbs would force them to walk themselves across the border. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your sworn testimony that they were shot and were taken from the scene of the shooting in a KVM ambulance directly to the border where they suffered and endured the treatment you described in your direct the other day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you therefore be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see Mr. Marcussen on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This comes a little late but I was scrambling to find the right rule. I should have known this by heart. It appears Mr. Ivetic intends to use a video to show that the witness was wrong with respect to these people in boiler suits. It would be my submission that if he's intending to impeach the witness on this he would have to show this piece of evidence to the witness this under Rule 90(H)(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't accept the submission for the Prosecution. We consider that the Rule has been complied with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I make a point please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not on this you can't, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on that, on what was said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the evidence. On this matter? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you in private now about something that's just been said because I have a real concern on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, general, with regards to the wounded OSCE personnel, would you be surprised to find out that, in fact, these individuals were actually evacuated from the scene of the shooting where they had been shot at by the KLA and were taken to Pristina hospital, where in fact they were treated --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And moved on to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was told to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And on the way to Macedonia they were also escorted and assisted by the MUP personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have had a police escort, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can see anxiety about the transcript, but if you pay attention to LiveNote, you'll be able to follow the transcript there until the matter is resolved. We can carry on with the evidence meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, these individuals one had a glass cut on the arm and one had a slight indirect gun-shot wound to the shoulder. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gun-shot wound to the shoulder was not life-threatening but it was more than a slight wound. You wouldn't like one like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't like any type of gun-shot wound. But the point is the incident was not as you implied the other day wherein they were taken from the scene directly to the border and while they were -- well, in the manner you described the other day, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main medical assistance they were given was in the ambulances by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Marcussen is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I mean, I don't recall the evidence being that the victims -- the wounded were taken straight from the place where the incident had taken place to the border. I don't think that had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He testified to that verbatim here today just before I had asked him if it would surprise him -- just before we went to closed session we asked if that's what his testimony was. You can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just carry on. We'll be able to sort it out in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, my recollection was they were put into the ambulances in which there were paramedics and they were treated immediately as they drove from the Decani area to Pristina. I know that they stopped in Pristina for a moment or two because I know that the head of mission spoke to them both at that stage and wanted to and because their injuries were not life threatening that was perfectly okay. They then went on to the border. If they had a police escorted, then I'm delighted. I wasn't made aware of that but I'm not surprised -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The point is, sir, what you described the other day, the wounded men having to walk by themselves across the border and being subjected to this, that never actually happened, did it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was how it was relayed to me, yes, it was, that the paramedics were not allowed to go over the border in the vehicles with the wounded men because were they to do that, their passport, their visas, which were one-way, one entry visas would have been stamped and they wouldn't be allowed back in and we would have lost a significant part of our medical cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to a meeting you discussed with General Lukic and in discussing your meeting, you made reference to P2544 which memorialises this meeting which occurred on or about the 24th of December, 1998. In reading this exhibit it seems to indicate that you started off the meeting complaining that, in fact, you had not been invited previously by General Lukic for an earlier meeting. Is that really how you started this meeting, complaining about not receiving an invitation to meet with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says that I stated we should have met earlier. Is that a -- that's not a complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at the next sentence, he stated that "the reason they had not was due to an absence of an invitation from General L which exemplified the lack of cooperation that was about to be discussed." It sure sounds like a complaint.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It was not one of my huggy-feely meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, under the auspices of the KVM agreement, there were General Loncar and others from his commission available to you, specifically Colonel Mijatovic, the MUP liaison, as well as local area and local-level MUP liaisons at each of the various RCs. Now, Mr. Lukic was not part of Loncar's commission, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Article 9 of the general agreement about the KVM stipulates that contact is to be through liaison officials that are to be assigned. Mr. Lukic was not, in fact, a liaison official, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was why the meeting had not taken place until then, and had the arrangements that had been set in place been adequate, then the meeting might not have been needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that every meeting that was sought by you with General Lukic was, indeed, granted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, one of the themes that was discussed at this meeting was the issue of Malisevo, and you've identified that in your -- in your witness statement. I'd like to address some of the testimony that you have in there. Isn't it correct that the Burns-Djordjevic agreement, that is to say, the agreement between the KDOM and the MUP, that that particular agreement specifies that forces -- that the Serbian MUP police is to withdraw its forces from various villages and to localise them in the village or town of Malisevo so that the concentration of MUP personnel in Malisevo was foreseen and not limited by the Burns agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall the Burns agreement, it allowed for -- it named 27 locations, of which nine could be occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe we're mixing apples and oranges here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P394 up on the screen, that way you can convince yourself that the parts that I'm reading are accurate. But section 3 of the Burns agreement says: "The police will withdraw its stationary forces from Dragobil, Ostrozub, Opterusa, Dobrodelan, Studencan, Samodreza, Pecane and Klecka and will keep them in Malisevo, Orahovac, Zociste, Restane, Suva Reka, and Dulje. So I ask you again, sir, isn't it a fact that the Burns agreement specifically foresaw and did not call for a reduction or a withdrawal of the police presence in the town of Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's paragraph 3. Yeah, I read that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now that we're on the same page, isn't it therefore correct that what you were seeking, that is to say, reduction of the police in Malisevo, was actually seeking a modification of this Burns-Djordjevic agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where in the Burns-Djordjevic agreement does it say what the force level is in Malisevo, then, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, whether in fact your request to ask for a reduction of the police in Malisevo was something that would have to cause for the Burns agreement and the Geremek-Jovanovic agreement to be amended and modified?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my understanding because we weren't talking about withdrawing, we were talking about reducing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This exchange started on the basis of a question that suggested the forces had to be withdrawn from certain villages and to go instead to Malisevo. This agreement says something rather different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That they could keep them in Malisevo, Orahovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not the ones from the other villages but the ones that were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's rather different from the first question you posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I might have misspoken. That was my intention -- understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we heard testimony from General Loncar that in fact the issue of reducing the police in Malisevo had been forwarded to the entire Federal Commission for their consideration in Belgrade, whether they would have to amend the agreements to make this happen. Do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't ever recall anyone suggesting that these agreements were going to need to be amended, no, never ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if the evidence shows that other persons within the KVM did know that and did seek to have it amended by going through the Federal Commission, would knowledge of that fact that you don't know change your appraisal of General Lukic's abilities with respect to Malisevo, as set out in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because General Lukic was the head of the police in Kosovo, so one had this wild irrational idea that he was in charge of the police. Tell me if I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are, sir. You don't, in fact, have any knowledge of the structure and the operation of the police forces in the Republic of Serbia, the various divisions, the various structures in place, and how the police operates, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Lukic had not had the ability to make a decision about the actual level of policing inside Malisevo, then I assume he would have told me that and he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you're basing everything on an assumption. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the benefit of as many lawyers as we have in this courtroom. I was having to make it up as I went along; you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've also had sworn testimony from a commander Zyrapi of the KLA that in fact Malisevo was the main KLA route for smuggling of weapons into Kosovo from across the border. Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have said it was the main route; I would have said it was one of the routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. As one of the routes, sir, wouldn't that justify a police presence in that locale to try and limit this illegal activity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think we've all agreed by looking at paragraph 3 that that's entirely legitimate and allowed. My conversation, I keep coming back to it wasn't whether or not there was a police presence, it was how oppressive it was, how big it was, how in your face it was, and we were attempting to reduce it in order to calm the situation and we were offering to put verifiers into the village in order to help with that situation, and that we eventually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the translation again. Now, sir, in -- now, sir, in your statement you talk about the patrols that were undertaken and the fact that armoured personnel carriers or APCs were utilised. Isn't it correct that paragraph 2 of the Burns-Djordjevic agreement actually authorised the MUP to utilise patrols, even employing APCs and armaments of up to 7.9 millimetre machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which would be used exclusively in self-defence and with restraint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm observing that there was a condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think the reason there was a condition was that there had been armoured vehicles used with machine-guns that had not been used in self-defence and had not been used with restraint, and that's why it was so specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. And these patrols in question were accompanied by your verifiers in their vehicles, as another witness testified here, specifically with respect to this area, since at that time Malisevo was in the -- within the confines of the Suva Reka municipality. Isn't it correct that the KVM vehicles escorted the police patrols on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We accompanied them in some cases, not exclusively. On a case-by-case basis as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You talk about the stops that were undertaken by the police in Malisevo to check IDs, et cetera, and to stop vehicles. Are you aware of the fact that Article 3, section 3 of the Geremek-Jovanovic agreement explicitly authorises trafficking crime stops and excludes such -- excludes a review of such activities from the purview of the KVM mission that you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And how were we to distinguish between a police roadblock that stopped people in order to attempt to deal with organised crime and one that was stopping them to shake them down for their pocket money without being prior informed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Utilising properly trained police verifiers instead of military verifiers would be one way, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or being psychic, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you answer my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we got police verifiers we used them, of course we did; until then, we used the people we had. And where we had people who had a military police background, we used them in preference to people who didn't have a military police background. I was not able to conjure policemen out of mid-air, and it's a well-known phenomenon of international operations that the police take a very long time to arrive in any force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can turn specifically to some of the staff that you had on hand. Am I correct that Mr. Guy Sands, Mr. Richard Heaslip and Mr. Viktor Ravishenko [phoen] who I believe preceded Guy Sands as the MUP liaison, these men were all three of them, all were of a military background. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the -- I think it was the Ukrainian had a military police background to the best of my knowledge, but yes, these were military people essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. And these three named persons -- these above-named persons as well as the other MUP liaisons met with the individuals and some met with Mr. Lukic. For instance, General Heaslip met with Mr. Lukic on multiple occasions. Would you say that he met with Mr. Lukic more than you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
