utterances.text: Yes, because Heaslip worked for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You would have to defer to these individuals that had daily interaction with the MUP with respect to appraisals of what the information was that the MUP provided to them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the context and what you're about to invite me to sign up to. I don't think I would blanket accept that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to sign up for anything; I'm asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied on, in particular, Heaslip to be my liaison with the MUP because he was assigned to it almost exclusively, and it needed someone to be assigned to it exclusively. I didn't have the time to do any one thing exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as the MUP observation points are concerned, am I correct there was one grand inspection of all the MUP observation points conducted, I believe, on the 5th of January, or thereabouts 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel Ciaglinski in his testimony claimed that on that inspection almost 40 observation points, instead of 27, were found and that they were all manned. That is not, in fact, what the findings of the inspection revealed, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do -- I wasn't actually in Kosovo at the time. This happened while I was back on a few days' leave. But my -- my instructions while I was away was to check every one of the 27 to make sure that no more than nine were occupied, as per the Burns agreement. And the message that I got when I got back was that they had indeed been inspected and that more than nine were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. But there was no discussion of 40. Let's clear that up first.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall 40 because that number --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doesn't make sense, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- isn't relevant. If it was more than nine, it was noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's your opinion that that would be noncompliance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, the Burns agreement that you have referenced states that the overview of the observation points will be completed by October 29th, 1998. Do you know what happened on October 29th, 1998, when Mr. Burns met with General Djordjevic of the MUP and re-evaluated how many of these observation points were actually going to be manned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Don't you think that since your mission was there to verify this agreement, it would be a crucial point to find out what the final understanding and final agreement of the parties was with respect to how many observation points could be manned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're telling me that the Burns-Djordjevic agreement that we have on the screen and which was well-known to every member of the KVM was somehow changed by a private deal, yeah, you're amazing me. And how would we have known of this private deal anyway? And if that had been the case, it would have been a really spiffing idea for someone to have told us that, not least someone on the MUP side. And they never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You also didn't have knowledge of the communications between KDOM and the MUP with respect to the base level of forces. So could this be another area that no one asked KDOM or KDOM didn't provide the proper information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think KDOM are in the dock here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to turn to another matter that Colonel Ciaglinski testified about, and I think you also -- you also testified regarding your return to Pristina following the Kumanovo agreement and that you found a burning heap of documents which coincidentally Colonel Ciaglinski said he examined alone with his interpreter. But in any event you said that you and Colonel Ciaglinski inspected this. Now, am I correct or is Mr. Ciaglinski correct that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to Ciaglinski's evidence on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe he testified about it multiple times. I don't have a page reference for it. I can remove the reference to Mr. Ciaglinski and just say am I correct if that would move things along.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, am I correct that the documents that were in this burning heap included completed application forms for both passports and ID documents as well as ID documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite possible. I mean, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were there. Did you see those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me put this in context. First of all, I was with Ciaglinski. He and I were a team together at this stage because we were attached to NATO. I was no longer chief of operations of the OSCE mission. I was attached to NATO KFOR as a liaison officer and Ciaglinski was there with me and that was it; we were a team of two. He drew my attention to the burning heap of documents, and therefore I assume he would have got there first, seen it, and then said, You need to come and see this. So I went there. So it's perfectly possible that he saw it first on his own and then he went and got me. I think that's probably what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did that heap of documents include completed application forms for passports and ID documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have done; it may have included shopping lists. But it did include some identity papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Colonel Ciaglinski testified that he removed some exemplars of these documents and safe-guarded them, and then gave them to you for further safekeeping. Is that true; and if so, where are these documents and why have they not been turned over to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Tribunal didn't exist in its current form in June 1999. I turned them over to the security detachment of the headquarters Ace Rapid Reaction Corps, which was KFOR, which was the appropriate authority in the chain of command I was in at the time, and you would need to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it you don't know what happened thereafter to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you have occasion, either from your own observations or through the translator, to determine whether in fact the identification documents you examined from the pile, what time period they were from. Were they current? Were they old? Expired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my recollection that the ones we looked at that had dates of birth on them had dates of birth around the 1950s. That was as much examination as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did they have anything on the cover? Did they say SFR Yugoslavia in Cyrillic and Latin script?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Most of the script was Cyrillic I seem to remember, but I cannot remember the exact details and these papers were pretty charred. We didn't go through the whole thing. We looked at it, realised what we believed them to be, and reported it to those who were in a better position to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. I've just one more area to ask you about, and I think I can probably condense it to one question. General, upon the withdrawal of the KVM from Kosovo-Metohija, I understand that on March the 27th, 1999, at one of the locations within Djakovica, where the KVM had been billeted and based, among the equipment left behind radio locators were discovered with radio locator antennas. Now, it is my understanding that these devices are used to mark targets, that is to say, they are left by targets, and then at some point in time later they are activated so as to guide missiles and bombs and other ordnance to the target. What was the KVM using these devices for, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not got the foggiest notion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, general, for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General Drewienkiewicz, I just have some few questions to clarify some matters that have come up during cross-examination. Maybe I should start with some of the things that have been discussed today. Now, did the KVM request a base-line from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you receive one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you try through other means to then establish the information you felt was needed for you to get a replacement for a base-line sent through?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by going out and looking, but it was much more difficult with MUP than with military because they go around in ones and twos or threes and fours, not in formed units. So they were a much more difficult set of people to track. And you heard I had hardly any policemen to do it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What kind of information would you have expected -- what kind of information should there have been in the MUP base-line so that it could serve its purpose in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we would have very much liked to have been given would have been a list -- first of all, a schematic of the chain of command so that we knew who was in charge at every location; what the locations were; what their state of manning was; and what, if any, were the heavy weapons that were at each of those locations, and we didn't receive any of that. And, indeed, also the details of rotation of police in and out of Kosovo, because that was going on, we were aware that people in some cases came into Kosovo for about three weeks on detached duty from the rest of Serbia and then returned to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, were you ever told that the KDOM had received any information about the MUP that would serve as a base-line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were told, Oh, that has all been handed over, and I would say, So to whom? Oh, it's all been handed over. That was the detail we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Even if you had been told that there were 10.021 MUP personnel in Kosovo, would that have been a base-line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would have wanted to know which locations they were operating out of in -- in what strength. And we would want to know, as I mentioned, what the rotation was so that it was not possible to add or subtract hundreds of policemen to or from this figure, simply by driving extra people in. We would expect to have known that when there was a rotation that 40 -- a bus load was going out and a bus load were coming in and that was the sort of information we never got. So it may have been a 1.021 but it could have been 1.121 a week later for all we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were efforts made by -- to your knowledge, were efforts made by the KVM to establish, for example, how many police stations there were in Kosovo and their location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain how that determination -- how you tried to reach a determination of this issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by driving around and observing from the outside, because I must also make the point that police stations were another place where we weren't allowed in routinely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to -- if you would have a look at Exhibit P667, please, if you can call that up. Are you able to see this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, is this a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can go down to see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the gentleman who signed the -- this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not specifically. I know he was on the distribution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you hold on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this document was used in direct or cross. I'm a little surprised it's being used in re-direct now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would submit, one, that it was one of the documents that I undertook to make submissions on the relevancy of later on. I think it was that we would -- yeah, I would make written submissions on the relevancy. The reason I'm putting it to the witness now is there's been an issue whether or not the MUP assisted KVM, providing information. What this document shows is that KVM was trying to get information about the number of police stations in a certain area; that information was forthcoming, and then it turned out when the KVM went out in a certain area to see what the situation was on the ground they found additional police stations. So I think it's relevant to the issue of cooperation that has been raised by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've now told the witness what you expect him to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think it follows from the document really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Which isn't ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the other hand, the approach that you're taking seems perfectly legitimate, and you should be allowed to follow this line since it arises out of a matter in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the date is significant, if we look at the date. If you scroll up to see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So what you're seeing from this is that as late as the 16th of March, we were still trying to find out what the base-line was. We evacuated four days later, so if this is to be shown as a shining example of MUP cooperation, I would say it came a little late, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can we scroll down to the bottom again so we can see the signature block and the distribution list. Could we go -- at least on my copy we cannot see the left part of -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, who is Kessler?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kessler is the deputy head of mission who was responsible for policing, to whom I handed over as many of my policing responsibilities or -- of the responsibilities that I'd taken on over policing as quickly as I could as soon as he arrived, which was late January or maybe early February. I was extremely pleased to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And we already talked about who Heaslip was. Now, in the two paragraphs, there's one paragraph that begins with in regional centre -- well, in RC-5, and there's a description of reporting on a number of police stations. And then in the next -- in the next paragraph there's a description of the KVM finding some additional police stations upon an inspection. Now, to your recollection, is -- does this reflect the way you carried out your operations at the time in order to try to establish a base-line? You would go to a place and be given information and then you would go out and inspect for yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was how we ended up having to do it. The ideal would have been to have received this from someone in the chain of command, higher up in the chain of command, which we could have distributed. This is an extremely labour-intensive way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, are you satisfied that this document is a correct description of -- would be a correct description of what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have to say I hadn't seen the document before. I do recall a conversation in which extra police stations were described as popping up, but I didn't focus on it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move over to another thing which is related to an exhibit which is not on -- which hasn't been used in direct and hasn't been used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So maybe before I get into that I should inform the Court why I'm doing this. An issue has been raised about the gentleman that the witness said he saw wearing these grey all covers or whatever the term was and I would like to show -- ask the witness first whether or not he remembers these gentlemen had -- were wearing any insignia or patches.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember noting that they were wearing sewn-on patches on to their -- on to their coveralls, and these patches, I recall, had the usual colours of red, white, and blue and either wings or daggers on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I were to show you some patches, do you think you might be able to recognise the patch if you see it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have a go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P1323, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the patch you see resemble any of these?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can we see the -- that's interesting. I thought there would have been a second page to this exhibit; that's obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the patch resemble any of these ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, why don't we have an exhibit with the colour of the uniforms since that's what was discussed in direct and in cross. I think that this type of fishing expedition is a little bit improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by an exhibit with the colour of the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness testified that he saw uniforms of a specific colour and a specific appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He also has mentioned in response to questions just now patches and there's no reason why this cannot be pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only one it resembles, to the best of my recollection, is the bottom right-hand one, the one marked 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The one marked 13, but you're not able to say whether this is actually the one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is the film that you were going to present in the system?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honour, that is why I couldn't present it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was about to ask for it to be shown to the witness. It would be very helpful to us if that were to happen so we're not left in a state of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I intend to use it with Maisonneuve who's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll appreciate that the point will undoubtedly be devalued if this witness has not had an opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is a video that was utilised in the opening statements that I was not able to track down. I've found a web link last night that had it on the internet but I do not have a copy that I would be able to use today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Something I don't like about the procedure here is that the Defence don't have any obligations to intimate their lists of witnesses or exhibits prior to the conclusion of the Prosecution case, and that's what gives rise to this situation which is a very unfortunate situation. Exhibits of this nature should be -- in an ideal situation, would be available for the Prosecution and the Judges to put to the witness to help with clarification of the point. So it's a matter for you because the Rules don't oblige you to do it, but it would greatly assist us if material of this nature that's going to be referred to later was in the system when the witness being challenged is giving evidence. If the Defence don't want to put it then they're not obliged to either, but it would help the party -- the Judges to be able to do it themselves. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'd just like a clarification at page 61, line 6. I thought I had heard the witness answer not the one marked 13 but the transcript shows him saying the one marked 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said the one marked 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bottom right-hand one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, General, I'm going back to the base-line just for one question. You were asked at page 25, line 6, today whether you were aware of any mistakes being made in the reporting regarding the MUP because of the lack of experienced policemen among your verifiers. The kind of information you needed for the base-line that you explained, so a list of equipment, locations, these sort of things, would that kind of information be something that somebody with a military background could also take in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, yes, because it was about chains of command and equipment and numbers and those sort of aspects are common to all of these sort of organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'll now move back to some issues that arise from the evidence yesterday. My learned friend Mr. Sepenuk asked you some questions that I'd like to seek some clarification on. At paragraph -- at page 7924, lines 3 through 17, you were being asked about the meeting that occurred on the 27th of November with Ojdanic. And I'll read out a question for you. What was being said there was: "During your briefing or the proofing that you had with Mr. Marcussen and others, in that supplemental statement little paragraph E you said: 'During the meeting on 25th November,' it's actually I think a mistake. I think it means the 27th November. Let's assume that during the meeting of 27th of December [sic] General Ojdanic did not say no to KVM inspectors and you left the meeting with him saying that the next meeting would be with the Pristina Corps to implement further details regarding inspections to establish a base-line, but you did not receive the information you wanted because it turned out that there was a difference of interpretation between the OSCE and the Serbian political leadership as to what was required under the agreement. Do you recall that?" And you answered: "Yes." Now, just to clarify for your sake, what is referred to as a supplemental statement is -- well, we call it a supplemental information sheet, but it's not an actual statement so I don't think that was being suggested. But we have tried to give the Defence a record of some issues that have come up during proofing. Now, in the operational part of this supplemental information sheet it actually reads as follows: "During the meeting on 25th," that should be 27th, "but during the meeting on the 25th of November, 1998, see paragraph 63, General Ojdanic did not say no to KVM inspections. General Drewienkiewicz left the meeting with General Ojdanic thinking that the next meeting would be with the Pristina Corps to implement further details" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly slow down for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My apologies. "General Drewienkiewicz left the meeting with General Ojdanic, thinking that the next meeting would be with the Pristina Corps to implement further details regarding the inspections to establish a base-line. At the meeting on 9th December 1998, see paragraph 81, however, Sainovic refused to allow KVM to carry out inspections."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So now my question is this: The difference between the two summaries you say in proofing is whether or not there was a -- you have knowledge of a difference of interpretation between the OSCE and the political leadership or whether you simply came to the meeting on the 9th and found out that Sainovic was refusing the KVM to carry out inspections. So --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you have information that -- is it your evidence that the dispute was between the OSCE and the Serbian political leadership exclusively?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I really think he answered that question. He said yes. That was the question. He answered it yes. And I don't know where the confusion is. I don't think this is proper re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, the -- something was being put to the witness as being his statement, which included things that -- I mean might be flowing from the summary of his statement but isn't from the statement. I'm trying to clarify what the witness's evidence is on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I admire the witness's mental agility if he's still with you. Why couldn't you just ask the question at line 8 which you've asked without going over all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'll ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not the point that you want answered and with respect to Mr. Sepenuk's objection I repel that because I think the question is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General -- well, maybe we should go about it in a different way. General, do you know who decided that you could not - and "you" meaning the KVM - could not carry out inspections as you wished to do them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was given to the head of mission with me there by Mr. Sainovic who, as far as we were aware, and we had certainly been led to believe, represented the Serbian government. So he was there as the representative of the Serbian government and he said, No inspections, among other things. He didn't talk about interpretations; he said: No inspections. There will be no inspections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you know whether anybody from the military was against inspections or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, by his body language, I got the firm impression that General Loncar was as surprised as we were. I was later told, I think by General Loncar, that the message had come from the General Staff in Belgrade but I never attempted to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would it be a fair interpretation of that answer to say you don't know what the position of General Ojdanic was on this issue or General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I have no direct evidence, nobody -- neither of them ever said those things to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, following this question from Mr. Sepenuk, you were asked about paragraph 65 and 66 of your statement, and maybe you would want to just remind yourself of what's in those paragraphs. If you -- do you still have the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is about the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- noted issue. You said that you didn't fully recollect these things and would need to consult your notes. Did you bring your notes with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I had a look to see -- I looked through what I have for December with me, and I only brought about 10 kilos with me this time and I didn't bring my notebooks with me and I think it's in my notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What I would like -- the thing is that we have actually as a Defence exhibit these notebooks. It is D -- sorry, it's 3D412. It's a rather big exhibit, but the relevant parts -- I've excerpted part of this which is pages 310 to pages 324.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe the usher would be kind enough to assist and give the witness a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, what I'd -- is this one of your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, the entry -- we have the first page of the notebook, book 3. And if you go to the second page there's an entry -- I think it's from the 24th of November. I see we actually have it in e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please, sorry, in -- for e-court. I think we'll -- in e-court I think we got to a wrong page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this -- the one I've --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You have something different --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got something completely different. I'm blessed if I know what that one's from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we can deal with it -- this in a different way. Could you look through the pages that I have provided to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And tell me whether those pages are your notes covering before the meeting on the 27th, of the 27th, and after the 27th, so basically these are the notes from the relevant period in time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that there are no notes that you made during the meetings in your handwriting from the meeting there are no notes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you go to R0161462, you can see that there's typed stuff that was there when I went in, then there is some heavy handwritten stuff that I'm pretty sure I wrote before we went in and then there's some other stuff that I was writing at the time as we had the meeting. So there's bits of -- there's different bits of it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I should just explain to the Court that's looking on something that looks rather mystical I think on the screen right now that I think there's been an error in the way this exhibit was scanned in the Defence. We have forwarded some clean pages of this which actually have the proper text on it. So we will have -- if the Defence agrees to update this particular exhibit in e-court we will have a proper copy later on in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My question is this: I think it was being suggested that because there was no records -- well, I'm getting to the question now. General, I think the point that was made yesterday is that it doesn't say "noted" anywhere on this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I take it that apart from the things you have written in your handwriting during the meeting, there was a lot of other things being said at the meeting that is not noted down here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, when you made your statement in 2000, you said that General Ojdanic had said that these issues were noted, were you making the statement on the basis of your memory of the meeting rather than on the basis of your notes. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm pretty sure that he said "noted" because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm going to object to this. Yesterday he clearly said that this paragraph -- I put the whole paragraph to him and he said: Yes, this is one of the few instances -- at least I said this is one of the few instances where you may have gotten it wrong, sir. And he said: Yes, I may have gotten it wrong. And I'm not sure of the purpose of the questioning now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, the fact that the matter may come out differently in re-examination is not a cause for not admitting the evidence. What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That he's testified to this and I don't -- and I don't see the point of re-direct examination. I don't think it's proper under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the whole point of re-direct on points that he's testified on to clarify them if there's a legitimate point to be clarified. On the face of it this is one now that we see the state of the notebook, at least the copy that's been scanned into --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Which has very resemblance to what we have, I might say. The chicken scratchings there and what not is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And indeed, in fairness the witness has the original in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it may be clearer for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, just before we move on, I can't see that this is objectionable; it's a matter that can be resolved by comment in due course when we come to review the evidence. It is important, Mr. Marcussen, that you ask open questions. That's the only observation I have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please let's get this -- let's get to the point quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No -- well, I think we are at a point where I can simply ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it your recollection, after having actually been shown your notes from the relevant periods, and maybe having thought about it overnight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds like a leading question coming. Let's interrupt it before you make it such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, paragraph 65 of your statement, does that correctly reflect your memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a leading question. If you want an answer to something that you seek to use in contradiction of evidence given in cross-examination, you will have to ask an open question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If you remember, what did Ojdanic say at the meeting when you put forward the request to be able to verify -- carry out inspections in barracks and in other locations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say yes and he didn't say no; and frankly, I wouldn't have expected him to. He said -- I mean, the word "noted" is shorthand for, you know, let's look at it. He didn't say "no." I didn't come out of that meeting feeling that I had had a completely hopeless meeting. It -- my impression of it at the time was that it gave me the -- the green light to go to the next level in his chain of command and open discussions with them, which was really the whole purpose of -- of the meeting. And because he'd only just taken over, I didn't expect him to be as forthcoming as perhaps his predecessor might have been, who had been in the job for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next passage of cross-examination yesterday concerned the next paragraph in your statement. Do you remember what General Ojdanic said about the rotation of VJ in and out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- he made the point that they did do rotations, that it was normal business, it was part of being a conscript army, and that we were welcome to monitor those change-overs, to make sure that everybody understood that a certain number were coming in and a certain number were going out, and there was no net difference. Now, that was a proposal -- I think that was as far as we probably got with that one at the time. And I think my paragraph 66 I don't think is completely accurate at this stage, looking back on it. I think it was relayed to me that it had been refused later, and I think I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't recollect you saying that yesterday, but perhaps you'd -- I mean my note is quite clear that Mr. Ojdanic did indicate a willingness to look at this issue at the time, which is quite different from what is said in the statement. But I don't recollect you saying that you later heard it had been refused. Now, have I missed that yesterday, do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With huge respect, I think you may have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, that was clarified by the General yesterday that it was not General Ojdanic who gave any comment. The comment that it was refused by General Ojdanic is simply not so. The General testified yesterday that that message was relayed to him by General Loncar as coming from General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That does complete the picture for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is at page 7926, lines 5 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you have other issues to explore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have a few. Maybe it's time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it is time. We have to break again for reasons which, no doubt, have been explained to you. So could you leave the courtroom again, but we're going to restrict this break to 20 minutes since we had a longer one earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at just after ten minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, yesterday Mr. Ackerman discussed with you how you conduct -- rather, how terrorists sometimes operate and he mentioned -- or he asked you whether it was a common tactic that they would operate from, he called it, civilian enclaves and then leave and then go out and then claim that there had been an attack on civilians. He asked: Is that a common tactic; and you said: Yes. My question is, as we have been discussing tactics and you might offer some insight on this: What kind of tactics do you employ as being the law enforcement side of this kind of a conflict to avoid these sort of claims by the insurgent side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please. Again we have an objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that the witness testified in cross-examination that he did not have any kind of training in police work. I believe that is what is law enforcement, so I don't know how you can ask him for what kind of tactics one would employ if the gentleman is not trained in that area and said that he did not have any personal experience in that area. So I think that it's an improper question. It's an area that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say I don't understand the question. Can you clarify what it is you're actually trying to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe I can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, as -- how would the authorities of a sovereign state conduct operations so as to avoid or minimise allegations by civilian -- by the insurgent forces that they had been attacking civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would say that I do feel that I can answer this because this isn't police work necessarily, it's work that armies do get called in to do in aid of the civil power. In those circumstances, the -- the principles you use are minimum necessary force and operating within the law. And as, perhaps, an illustration. In the time that the British Army has been in Northern Ireland since 1969, I'm not aware that we have ever used artillery. We've never used aircraft, launched weapons, nor have we ever used tank main armament in any of these circumstances. They've always been long-barrelled weapons, rifles, that have been used or at -- at best, a machine-gun. But generally, when someone fires a lethal weapon, every round is recorded, and you have to account for every round. And so it's a much more constrained sort of operation than the sort of operations that we witnessed -- that I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Another issue we have touched upon - and I think that was both yesterday and today - is the extension of the border zone from 500 metres to 5 kilometres and then to 10 kilometres. From a military perspective -- from a military perspective does it make a difference whether the border zone is 5 or 10 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it makes life easier for the people trying to police the border because if you have the bigger border zone you have, you can enact legislation so that people have to have a reason to be in that border zone. So it's a great help to the forces of law and order. But if you go out 10 kilometres from the border in Kosovo, you're up against some quite substantial settlements that would need to be subject to that regime as well. So it would have been very difficult to operate it. I think there are areas where the main Prizren to Pec, the north-south road in that area, I think that runs within 10 kilometres of the border on occasion. So it would cut that. So it would be a very difficult one to enforce, but it would make the life of the people trying to police the border quite a lot easier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If your concern were a NATO force ground invasion, would it make a difference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because you could -- I mean, you could in theory move everybody out of that border exclusion zone who lived in it. There is no end to the things you could do in an exclusion zone once you've declared it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- how did the extension of the border zone affect the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we learned of it through I think Bo Pellnas in Belgrade who obtained a copy of the relevant Official Gazette, but we were very surprised that no one had formally discussed it with us because clearly it was going to make a big impact on the way we did our business. And one would have thought -- would certainly have required discussion if not amendment to the various agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But what was the impact, if any, on the way you conducted or could conduct your operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- we discussed it and we agreed that since we hadn't been consulted we weren't going to obey it. So we just got on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were you, indeed, allowed to get on with it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were stopped much more in that border zone and harassed a lot more. So life became a lot more difficult in trying to work out what was happening inside that border zone -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To the extent that you were able to move in the border zone, did you notice whether the extension of the border zone had any impact on the population in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see people formally being moved out from villages to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my last few questions concern something that came up during Mr. Cepic's cross-examination. You were asked about Podujevo and there was an exchange which related to whether or not the KLA had ever taken Podujevo itself, and you said to your knowledge that had never happened. And then you said - and just for the reference it is at page 7938, lines 18 to 22 - you said: "What was happening in February and March was not what was happening in November/December. We were not trying to verify" -- sorry. "We were not trying to verify an agreement of October anymore. We were trying to hang on to the situation and stop it erupting into a full-scale war, so it was a quite different situation."

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, first, are you talking here about the time around Rambouillet and Paris talks? Is that around the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: While Rambouillet was going on, certainly at the start the level of violence did reduce substantially, and we noted that. Yes. And then from let us say the end of the third week of February, it started to stoke up again. And the situation then got considerably more exciting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So that would have been after the end of Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rambouillet sort of droned on and on. It stopped and they agreed to reconvene, and I would need to check but the main negotiations stalled after about ten days. There was then an agreement to meet again, and that happened I think in about the first week of March but I would -- I could easily be wrong by several days on either side. But once the main talks at Rambouillet had stalled, things got -- things hotted up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 87 of your statement -- sorry, 187, you discuss this issue of leaving feet on the ground and we get into this 15 companies issue. Was that around this time as well or was it at a different time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it was earlier. I would say that that was -- I would say that was around mid-January where I think I sort of wrote down somewhere we seem to be detecting a pattern which is that something happens, there is a large army and police force detached to wherever the place is, it deals with it, but not all people go back to barracks, they leave a foot on the ground. And these feet on the ground became the force that I described as 15 companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, going back to what I quoted before: "We were not trying to verify an agreement of October anymore. We were trying to hang on to the situation and stop it erupting into a full-scale war." What was that war between?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the -- the Yugoslav forces and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there also a concern -- was there -- was it also a concern that that would lead to the involvement of NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So what did you do in practical terms to try to avoid this eruption of war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that my statement about hanging on to the situation really reflects our attitude from -- from early January or even mid-December onwards. We were conscious that if we could continue to be present, that we were, to the greatest degree possible, a group that were able to damp down the situations and act as an interlocutor between the two sides. And we felt if we could buy the time for negotiation then it was still possible to come to a settlement through diplomatic means and we were all very passionate about wanting that and not letting small incidents escalate to the degree that NATO, which of course still had its activation order still uncancelled, did not -- did not get to a point where it felt the need to intervene through its activation order. And there were certainly sabre-rattling sounds from NATO on occasion that we hoped by being there we could avoid this thing becoming a shooting war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would I be interpreting this correctly to say that at this point in time the KVM was trying to do its best to avoid a conflict between the forces of the FRY and Serbia and NATO? Was that one aspect of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to avoid situations arising which could be interpreted in a way that NATO felt its mandate allowed it to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you tell any of your contacts on the Serbian side of these attempts and of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think I did, but I obviously had to be fairly circumspect about the extent to which I was criticising another international organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you think that the efforts of the KVM did actually succeed in -- in delaying the escalation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we bought time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, that completes your evidence to us. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence and to help our investigations. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the next witness to be coming on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, don't bring any witness in until I say that that's appropriate. If you have something to deal with, we'll deal with it quite separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Simply, at page 5174 Mr. Petrovic raised a concern about the translation of Exhibit P1335. All I want to say is we have gotten a new translation of this document, which has been uploaded into e-court. And the issue that Mr. Petrovic pointed out -- sorry, we are going to put it up into the system. We're going to leave the two translations there, but we want to avoid creating two separate exhibits. So there are going to be two English translations of this document in e-court. I'm saying this on record so that when one searches for this particular exhibit, this explanation is going to come up. I don't think I need to belabour the point anymore and waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which one are we supposed to have regard to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the first translation there was a -- between two slashes, there was an explanation of what something meant, whether an authority was to act on behalf of a Crisis Staff, and the issue was whether or not this document actually was an authority to -- a bank-type document giving authority to a person to access a bank account. That is actually what the document is. I can read -- it's just one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No -- well, it's completely out of context here. It's a matter that parties should try to resolve themselves, and if there is an issue here which can't be resolved then you'll need to make a filing or, alternatively, tell us quite simply which translation you're advancing as the correct one. It's for you to deal with these matters and put your position to us and now's not the time for that. There are mechanisms for dealing with these things. If they can be dealt with by discussion and e-mail, fine; if they can't be that way, you'll have to make a filing to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is no issue, it's just so the record is clear that there are two translations but point taken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who is the next witness? Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours, the next witness is K64 for whom I'd like to start by making an application for the withdrawal of protective measures which had been granted before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that all protective measures including the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Voice distortion, image distortion, and a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the name of the witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Ljubinko Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you spell the last name?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: C-v-e-t-i-c with a half diacritic on the last C.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any problem over that in the circumstances? Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness enters court I should like to raise a problem before the Chamber. I have consulted others as well when this problem is raised the witness should not be present. This concerns Exhibit P1468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a Prosecution exhibit, a Prosecution exhibit 1468. In the break I tried to ask Mr. Stamp, I, Mr. Petrovic, did whether they would be using it or not. At the time he didn't know so I don't know now. If he wants to use it, I have a series of objections to raise in regard to the usability of this document. If you took a good look these are some notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly speaking I haven't got a clue. It says meetings of the joint command but the author is -- you can't see the source of the document, the page numbers. I have -- I don't know whether this is an entire document, who prepared it, nothing is indicated, and then I can see that the witness who is coming has not attended any of these meetings. That means that there is some other documents, perhaps, that have not been signed which Mr. Stamp wants to exhibit but they are printed and you can see these details. This cropped up from I don't know where. This is somebody's handwriting. I don't know whether all the pages are there, whether it is a document in its entirety. You cannot just bring any old manuscripts here and say this is an exhibit. In particular you cannot present it to a witness who was never there. So this is my concern because in that way you can present anything you want so that is my objection to the usability of this exhibit. If he wants to use it will he please inform us what it really is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the objection might be a little premature. I could indicate that we have no present intention of using this document, having spoken to the witness recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear no intention of using the document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, indeed. And while the usher is bringing the witness, I confirm that the various protective measures granted in this case are revoked, in particular, the pseudonym and the voice and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Cvetic, the various counsel here -- please feel free to adjust these headphones yourself. If they are uncomfortable, just try to adjust them to make them comfortable. Various counsel here have questions for you, and the first person to ask questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, could you please tell us your full name and state your occupation, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubinko Cvetic, and currently I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I understand, Mr. Cvetic, that in 1990 you were appointed the head of the SUP for the jurisdiction of Kragujevac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just tell us what does the acronym "SUP" stand for.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you retired from the police.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of March this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do I understand it to be correct that you were the head of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica from January 1997 until the 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we look at the time when you were the head of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, can I just take you back to the period when you were head of the SUP of Kragujevac. Can you recall initiating an investigation into an incident in March of 1993 involving a senior member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was that member, if you could just tell us the name, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the investigation was in respect to what possible charge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: The Kragujevac police caught him poaching with a colleague of his from Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, was the investigation brought to any court proceedings or was it eventually stopped?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: It was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you a question which I just want answered in one way or another. As a result of these investigations that were initiated, do you believe that they had a good or a bad effect on your career in the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: I think that it actually affected my career adversely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you need to be asked any more questions about that we will. But can I now move on to your post b --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this just going to hang there or is it going to somehow or other get linked to something important?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is in some information by way of background. I just raise it in examination-in-chief because it is possible that there might be issues raised in cross-examination in respect to any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, what position do you think you would have reached in the SUP if this hadn't intervened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, after that incident, the then-deputy head of the public security service, Radovan Stojicic, a.k.a. Badza, called me and my deputy, Zivko Petrovic. Him, he relieved of office and sent him to be the head of the Prizren SUP and he was killed in a traffic accident in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now like to answer my question, which was: What position do you think you would have reached in the MUP if this hadn't happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the very least I would have remained the head of the Kragujevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying that movement -- your movement to Kosovska Mitrovica was demotion in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you arrived at the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP in January 1997. I take it that you met with your subunit commanders, who were working within that SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, if you can, what was the security situation in your SUP area or your SUP jurisdiction in 1997 when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the reports of the heads of police stations and the commanders of the police units, the security situation was very difficult and very complex, and this particularly concerned the terrorist activities that had been stepped up at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did this situation continue into 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the terrorist activities were, in fact, even more intensive then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about the structure of the MUP in Kosovo in 1998/1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And before I do could we put 25 -- Exhibit P2555 on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we're doing that can I ask you: In 1999 was anybody in particular appointed the head of the MUP in Kosovo -- sorry, 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, heading the staff of the MUP in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was that? Who was appointed to head the staff of the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: The head of the staff of the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. -- To that post was appointed Mr. Sreten Lukic on the 11th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you remember who were the other senior members of the MUP staff for Kosovo from 1998 to 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: In the staff there were a number of persons who were in charge of different fields, very narrowly specialised fields. The staff had its deputy chief, deputy head, and a certain number of persons in charge of different areas for crime, for economic crimes, for general crimes, for traffic, for commercial matters, for security, and logistics, and similar. There were a total of 14 persons on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll just ask you about two in particular. Who was in charge of the crime unit on the staff, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: There existed two types of crime that we had, that was general crime, crime generally speaking, and economic crimes, commercial crime. In charge of the commercial crime department was a person from the city SUP, and for the general crime department, a person from the SUP of Vranje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the general crime unit, who was the person -- can you name the person in charge of that unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was a person from the SUP of Vranje by the name of Novica Zdravkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the document on the screen, Mr. Cvetic, that is Exhibit P2555 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we have not been notified about the use of this document, so if my learned friend can explain why this has been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have we not seen this document in the case already?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the document was used --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the document was used during the opening statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you notify this as one of the exhibits to which the witness would be referred?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As soon as the witness was able to confirm it, as soon as he arrived here and was able to confirm it, we sent notification to the Defence, but this document is merely a chart which confirms what was in the statement. It's demonstrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Mr. Lukic is saying he hasn't had notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, I haven't seen one. We have a 65 ter notification. I have it -- one with me, and it's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The notification in respect to this particular document was sent yesterday. The witness arrived yesterday or the day before yesterday and was [indiscernible] to confirm this document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still we don't have that document on the list they sent regarding the court but not this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just cutting through that for the moment is there some prejudice to you caused by the use of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't know and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I saw many charts regarding the MUP structure, and I don't -- I don't know who composed this one and why is this composed in this manner. We have different charts given by the Prosecutor, and the structure has been completely differently depicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't prove anything. It's merely indicative of apparently what's in the statement. We remain concerned, as always, about the late intimation of material in this case, but it's not a change of front or anything of that nature that appears to have occurred. And therefore, I can see no prejudice in this being utilised to try to clarify points in the witness's evidence. Plainly, on its own, it is not evidence, and therefore it's difficult to see that it can cause you any prejudice so we will allow questions to be -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe if the witness can repeat this order then there is no need for him to see this chart because I can see really something illogical on this chart -- not something, many things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll have plenty of time to cross-examine on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in any event all the questions the witness has been asked so far don't bear any relation to what is on the chart, in spite of the fact that Mr. Stamp may have been seeking answers related to the chart. In any event we shall allow it to be used in the circumstances. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, you see the chart in front of you. Were you shown a chart yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And does it fairly depict the organisational structure of the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: This chart here depicts the ministry with two lines of work, namely the state security department and the public security department. As part of the ministries, also the secretariat of the ministry. And here it is attached to the public security department as far as I can see. It's the -- and the MUP staff for Kosovo has been shown as an intercommand between the MUP and the secretariat or the administration in Kosovo. As regards the secretariats in Kosovo, that is okay. These are the secretariats that were there. Now, special anti-terrorist units are linked to the MUP, whereas here they are linked to the MUP staff. That means that this is not a fair depiction. The operational groups, that is all right. Special police units, these were part of the Ministry of the Interior, the PJPs, that is the, or they were part of the individual secretariats. But when they were engaged in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, they were manoeuvreing forces and would be under the command of the MUP staff. The special operations unit was part of the state security department, as indeed shown here. The MUP staff, as far as I know, did not have command responsibility over the special operations unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I think we'll just take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who compiled this diagram?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This was compiled by an internal OTP department military analyst team on the basis of the information at our disposal including -- well, I've quite -- a broad spectrum of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can assist Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's compiled by a military analyst, Philip Coo, but not a police analyst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There existed operationally in Kosovo while you were there a special operations unit called the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo during 1998 and 1999, there was a special operations unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this unit was attached to the state security department, RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which department --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: It was attached to the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The state security sector is also known as RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: No. These are two separate sectors or departments within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, could you just please describe or just tell us which department was the special operations unit, the JSO, subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: Special operations units were subordinated to the RDB, to the state security department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope it's translation that's the problem, because we've come full circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in 1999, the special operations unit, the JSO, was engaged occasionally in operations in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC
utterances.text: You are using the plural, JSOs, whereas there was only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if some of the Serb speakers here can assist. It looks as though there is a failure to translate much of this accurately. Can anyone identify whether there's a particular problem? Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be easily dealt with. You see that Mr. Coo put the names here of people heading each of the departments. If you ask the witness what the name of the commander of the RDB was, perhaps he can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not the point I'm asking you, Mr. Fila, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we'll get the translation. That was the issue and a way to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out what's happened so far, because the word "department" was denied, as the superior body, and then later it was stated by the witness that it was the superior body. The real answer here is probably for Mr. Stamp not to ask leading questions, and then the witness will be able to give his own answers, which will be much more helpful.
